sentences: A barefoot friar stands on the rocks outside his cave, his arms spread wide as he gazes up at the sky.
Light pours in from the top left, making his body, the rocks and the distant fields glow.
This is Saint Francis in the Desert, painted around 1475 to 1480 by the Venetian artist Giovanni Bellini.
It is oil on panel, about 125 centimetres high and 142 centimetres wide.
It belongs to the Frick Collection in New York.
Francis of Assisi was a thirteenth-century Italian friar, and the religious order he founded still exists today.
Tradition says that in 1224, at the mountain hermitage of La Verna, he received the stigmata, the wounds of Christ.
Look closely at his open palms.
The marks of the wounds are only faintly visible.
Bellini painted no angel and no vision of the cross.
He shows the presence of God through light and nature alone, which makes the whole scene feel radiant.
Now look at the landscape.
The title says desert, but the place looks like a valley in the countryside near Venice.
A small town sits on a hilltop, and the fields are turning green with spring.
Search for the animals.
A heron, a donkey, a rabbit and a kingfisher are all hidden in the scene, and far off a shepherd tends his flock.
They go about their day, as if unaware of what is happening to the saint.
Francis loved the natural world like a family.
In his Canticle of the Creatures, he praises God through Brother Sun, who brings the day and gives us light.
The light in this painting feels like that song turned into a picture.
Look at the bottom left corner.
Bellini painted a small scrap of paper there, as if it had been stuck onto the scene, and signed his name on it.
It is a tiny, witty detail in a very large picture.
We do not know for certain who ordered the painting, or why.
The leading idea is that the Venetian nobleman Zuan Michiel commissioned it in the late 1470s, perhaps for a remote island church of Saint Francis in the Venetian lagoon.
By 1525 it already hung in the palace of Taddeo Contarini in Venice.
Centuries later the painting travelled to England and passed through several collections.
In 1915 it was bought by the American collector Henry Clay Frick, and it has stayed in his New York home, now a museum, ever since.
Step back and see the whole landscape.
While one man opens his arms to the light, the world around him carries on quietly as usual.
This morning, stand in the sunlight from your window for a moment and let it reach you.
